The radar frequency chosen for the straight wire experiment was 450 MHz, corresponding to a wavelength of 0.667 m.
The total length of the wire used in the RATSCAT experiment was 2.48 m, giving a length-to-wavelength ratio (kl) of 11.7.
The radius of the wire used in the RATSCAT experiment was 0.04 mm, ensuring that the condition ka << 1 was met.
The linearly polarized electric field vector of the radar was chosen in the plane formed by the wave vector k and the wire axis l, so that cos(ψ) = 1.
The accuracy of the RCS measurements was within about 3 dB at the peaks and degraded at the nulls of the RCS patterns.
Chu's expression was found to be accurate only at broadside incidence (90 degrees), but led to very erroneous results at all other angles.
Tai's original expression predicted the correct number of lobes in the RCS vs angle pattern and agreed with the data within a few decibels, except near the nulls, for kl values up to about 17.

The modified Tai expression, which introduced a function f(θ) to correct the broadside behavior, predicted the RCS within a few decibels over the entire aspect angle variation, except near the nulls, for 4.5 < kl < 17.
Van Vleck's expressions led to predictions that were within a few decibels of the RCS data at all angles greater than 20 degrees from end-on, and for all thin wires tested with kl > 4.5.
Ufimtsev's analytical expression yielded results that were comparable in accuracy to Van Vleck's expressions, with predictions within a few decibels of the RCS data for all kl values considered.

The BRACT computer program agreed with the experimental data within 1 dB and 1 degree in look angle for all the wire configurations tested, except for two cases where the differences were around 4 dB.
BRACT was used to calculate the RCS of a wire with kl = 157, and the results were nearly identical to those obtained using the closed-form expressions of Ufimtsev and Van Vleck.

The authors note that the deficiency in Van Vleck's theoretical predictions at end-on incidence are associated with approximations in the published expressions, and when the general expressions are used, the deficiency disappears.
The BRACT computer program is more flexible and can handle arbitrary wire configurations, including bent or distorted wires, whereas the analytical expressions are limited to straight, thin wires.

The analytical forms take about one minute of computer time to yield results for a given wire for all angles of incidence, while the BRACT program takes a little longer, depending on the length of the wire.
